pattern: Backtest volatility calculation bug: mean_reversion_backtest.py computed volatility as std of all returns in a 20-day window, but should use rolling std() like the calibrator. Fixed by pre-computing rolling_vol = returns.rolling(20).std() * sqrt(252) / 0.5, then filtering trades when rolling_vol > threshold. This aligns the backtest with the C489 calibrated thresholds (SPY:0.35, QQQ:0.45, AAPL:0.66) which were derived using the same rolling volatility computation.

QAE threshold calibration is asset-specific: SPY (threshold 0.35) shows +0.414 Sharpe improvement, QQQ (threshold 0.45) shows +0.222 improvement, but AAPL (threshold 0.50) shows -0.680 degradation. QAE helps mean-reversion on low-vol assets (SPY, QQQ) but harms high-vol assets (AAPL). The optimal threshold from calibration may still be suboptimal if it produces negative delta.

AAPL mean-reversion is fundamentally broken: classical Sharpe 0.082, QAE Sharpe -0.698. Even the 'optimal' threshold produces negative delta. This suggests the MR signal (RSI + BB) doesn't work on AAPL's price action in 2024-2026, or AAPL's volatility regime is too noisy for QAE filtering to help.

DTN/Bundle Protocol uses store-and-forward architecture where bundles are held in non-volatile storage when no next-hop exists, rather than dropped. Critical failure mode: storage exhaustion vs. bundle lifetime management — buffer bloat can create 'data black holes' where nodes appear functional but are dropping bundles due to prioritization/expiration policies. The reliability-capacity tension (infinite store vs. finite buffers) is the fundamental design constraint, not link connectivity.

Vector databases use approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) indexing because exact search is O(n) — infeasible at scale. HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) graphs provide O(log n) search with high recall. Tradeoff: indexing time vs query speed vs memory.

Vector similarity only works if embeddings are trained for the right task. A text embedding model trained on Wikipedia won't work well for code search. Domain alignment matters more than vector dimension.
Best RAG systems combine vector similarity with keyword filtering. Vector captures semantics, filters capture precision. Pure vector search fails on rare entities and exact matches.

Consensus algorithms (Raft/Paxos) and distributed caching (Redis/Memcached) are complementary patterns in distributed systems. Raft provides linearizable state machine replication through leader election and log replication — one leader, followers replicate, split-brain avoided by majority quorum. Redis provides distributed caching with persistence options (RDB snapshots, AOF logs) and data structures (strings, hashes, sorted sets). Key insight: caching is about locality, consensus is about agreement — they solve different problems. Caching reduces read latency by placing data closer to consumers; consensus ensures all replicas agree on the single source of truth. Tradeoffs: caching introduces stale reads unless combined with invalidation protocols; consensus adds latency (leader election, log replication) but guarantees consistency. Modern systems often combine both: Redis clusters use gossip + leader election for sharded replicas.

Neural Architecture Search (NAS) automates neural network design through three main approaches: (1) Search space design — from coarse-grained (cell-based) to fine-grained (operator-level); (2) Search strategy — reinforcement learning (Zoph \& Lee 2017), evolutionary algorithms (EvoNAS), or gradient-based differentiable search (DARTS); (3) Optimization objective — accuracy vs. latency vs. memory vs. multi-objective Pareto optimization. Key insight: NAS trades massive compute for architectural expertise, but recent work focuses on weight-sharing, one-shot models, and proxy tasks to reduce cost. The no free lunch theorem applies: NAS finds architectures optimized for specific constraints, not universal architectures.
